repos.title: Ranking Agreement Does Not Reveal Paragraph-Edit Agreement in Two Released Paper Acceptance Predictors
repos.paper_summary: This paper tests whether a fast logistic-regression surrogate, trained on PaperScorer ICLR acceptance labels, can select paragraph rewrites for two released 3-billion-parameter acceptance predictors. On 198 original ICLR papers, the surrogate's rankings correlate with the two predictors at 0.731 and 0.547 Spearman. On 3,321 checker-admitted paragraph rewrites, within-paper agreement on score changes is near zero between the surrogate and each predictor, and selection by the surrogate shows no detectable advantage over random choice. Edits were generated by GPT-6-Luna and passed automated invariant and semantic checks. The pre-specified tests used bfloat16 arithmetic; a post hoc 32-bit rescoring gave the same near-zero edit agreement. Choosing the best of five rewrites with a predictor raised its raw score by under two points out of 100 over random choice. Limitations: the edits are presentation-only, there is one surrogate and two predictors from one base model, the release's float16 vLLM recipe was not run, and a single-author audit judged six of 20 evidence removals invalid.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Predicting acceptance does not show which paragraph rewrites an evaluator rewards, so this paper tests that agreement directly.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluators and study design
digest_headlines.headline: A logistic regression surrogate and two released predictors score frozen paragraph-rewrite inputs under four pre-specified tests.

digest_headlines.heading: How often are the proposed edits valid?
digest_headlines.headline: Automated checks admit 70.5% of checkable paragraph edits, and a blind audit judges all sampled presentation edits valid.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Surrogate edit rankings show no detectable agreement with either target, and search gains stay near zero.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work on review feedback and text manipulation does not measure within-paper agreement between scorers on paragraph edits.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Agreement on original papers does not carry over to revisions, and the findings cover only presentation-only paragraph rewrites.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The surrogate tracks original-paper rankings but not checked rewrites, so revision tools should be validated against their intended evaluators.

digest_headlines.heading: Broader impact statement
digest_headlines.headline: The paper warns that automated scores should not alone guide publication decisions, and its planned release contains no author-facing optimizer.

digest_headlines.heading: Data and code availability
digest_headlines.headline: Analysis code and per-edit scores will be public, while manuscript text stays restricted to the editor and reviewers.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists configurations, prompts, search algorithms, model versions, sampling rules, and cost accounting for the study.

repos.title: EvoWorld: Towards Out-of-Sight World Evolution in Generative Video Models
repos.paper_summary:
EvoWorld is a framework for generating video in which an event changes the world, and the change is shown when the camera returns to a subject that was out of view. The paper also introduces EvoWorld-Data, about 12k generated videos of at least 10 seconds, and EvoWorld-Bench, a 120-case evaluation set. A vision-language model acts as a "brain" that observes each generated segment, tracks the world state, and writes the next prompt. A segment-autoregressive renderer then produces the video, using Identity-Anchored Attention, which biases revisit tokens toward retrieved subject tokens, and a two-stage training scheme: supervised learning with clean anchors, then online rollout training on self-generated context.

On EvoWorld-Bench, EvoWorld reaches 90.8% Core Task Success, which requires successful revisit, event realization, and full causal plausibility together. The best baseline, Evoke-Turbo, reaches 21.7%. EvoWorld scores 100.0% on revisit, 97.5% on event success, and 94.2% on causal plausibility (Evoke: 32.9%). Its visual score of 83.8 is the highest in the table. In the ablation, Core rises from 82.5% without IAA to 84.2% with IAA, and to 90.8% with Stage 2.

Limitations: the benchmark has only 120 cases, and scoring relies on VLM-based judging and verification.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Out-of-sight causal evolution requires video models to reason about event consequences, not only preserve visual history.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing long-horizon video models preserve consistency, but do not ensure unobserved worlds keep evolving.

digest_headlines.heading: EvoWorld: Data and Method
digest_headlines.headline: EvoWorld pairs a vision-language model brain with a video renderer, trained on a 12k-video dataset in two stages.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: EvoWorld reaches 90.8% Core Task Success, exceeding the second-best baseline by 69.1 percentage points.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Conclusion: EvoWorld improves out-of-sight causal evolution over recent video world models while keeping quality and consistency.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers data construction, benchmark screening, metric definitions, training settings, one-shot baselines, MiniMax-H3 results and limitations.

repos.title: TailSteer: Trajectory-Tail Steering for Drift-Resistant Multi-turn Image Editing
repos.paper_summary: TailSteer is a final-stage training framework that reduces cumulative drift in multi-turn image editing by steering only the late denoising steps of a base editor. The refined model is trained on its own on-policy rollouts, using unchanged source content as a preservation reference, so no curated ground-truth editing pairs are needed. Early steps are trained to match the frozen base model's velocity. Later steps blend that velocity with a preservation velocity toward a source-based endpoint, with the blend weight falling from 1 at the steering onset to 0 at the final step. The method is tested on FLUX.1 Kontext [dev], FLUX.2 [klein] Base 9B, SenseNova-U1.5-8B-MoT, and Qwen-Image-2.1. The paper reports substantially reduced drift over 15 to 20 editing turns. On FLUX.2 [klein] Base 9B, Qwen-IB EN changes by at most +0.47 across the tested steering onsets. Limitations: drift is measured only over 15 to 20 turns, training uses only identity and local edit families, and qualitative comparisons use one steering onset.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: One-shot editors accumulate small errors across repeated turns, so strong single-turn editing does not guarantee long-horizon editing.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior fixes add modules, change representations, or add memory, whereas TailSteer trains the base model's own denoising dynamics.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: TailSteer trains a copy of the base model on its own rollouts, steering only late denoising steps toward source-preserving endpoints.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Across four backbones, TailSteer reduces drift over 15–20 editing turns while keeping single-turn scores close to base models.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion says TailSteer reduces cumulative drift across FLUX, SenseNova, and Qwen while largely retaining base generative capabilities.

repos.title: Turns Matter: Advancing Streaming Video RL via Turn-Level Credit
repos.paper_summary:
TurnWise is a turn-level GRPO framework for streaming video RL that gives each response-or-wait decision its own advantage and weights decisions equally in the loss. For each trajectory, it scores every prefix with all later turns set to silence, subtracts the reward accrued before each turn, and normalizes the remaining return within the rollout group. Turn-mean aggregation averages token losses within each turn, then across turns, so output length does not set a turn's weight. No critic or extra rollouts are needed.

On Qwen2.5-VL-3B, TurnWise reaches 43.56 PAUC on ProactiveVQA, 21.59 Timing F1 on OVO-Timing, and 49.43 average accuracy on StreamingBench, which are 3.96, 3.87, and 0.69 points above the strongest non-TurnWise results. On Qwen3-VL-4B it reports 42.44, 11.15, and 58.96. Adding turn-mean aggregation to turn-level credit cuts repetition from 15.53 to 5.98 relative to credit-only training.

Limitations: experiments cover two Qwen backbones and three benchmarks, and the reward is the fixed PAUC-based scorer from MMDuet2. The alpha sweep tests only four correction strengths.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Shared trajectory-level advantages misassign credit to redundant replies and useful follow-ups in streaming video reinforcement learning.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior streaming video methods use trajectory-level GRPO, which broadcasts one advantage across all decision turns.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Silence-completed prefix scores give each turn a remaining-return advantage, and turn-mean averaging weights every turn equally.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments compare TurnWise with fine-tuned and reinforcement-learning baselines on three streaming benchmarks using two Qwen backbones.

digest_headlines.heading: Results and Discussions
digest_headlines.headline: TurnWise posts the best aggregate scores on all three benchmarks, reaching 43.56 on ProactiveVQA with the 3B backbone.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Turn-level credit without a critic supports higher-quality, better-timed and more selective streaming responses.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix derives the telescoping decomposition, the group-relative correction, the interpolation and warm-up schedule, and the dual-clipping loss.

repos.title: Agent-Driven Generative Priors for Pathology Image Synthesis and Segmentation
repos.paper_summary: The paper proposes a three-stage pipeline for pathology segmentation: agent-based quality screening of TCGA patches, generative pretraining on the screened patches, and a lightweight segmentation head. A pathology expert agent scores a labeled pilot set for cell presence, stain quality, and histologic clarity. A ResNet-50 regressor learns these scores and ranks an unlabeled pool, and quantile filtering yields TCGA-200K, which contains 217,030 patches. A Diffusion Transformer trained with flow matching on these patches supplies features from four blocks. A multi-level decoder fuses them for pixel-wise prediction under cross-entropy plus Dice loss. On PanNuke, the method reaches 55.46% mIOU and 68.81% mDICE, compared with 53.77% and 66.70% for UNI, the second-best method; both gains are marked significant (p<0.05). On PathSeg-380K, a 12-cell-type dataset introduced here, it reaches 55.45% mIOU (UNI: 54.59%) and 67.81% mDICE (Un-SAM: 66.33%), with no significance mark on these two metrics. Limitations: the authors note that agent screening is costly, and the curated data come from five TCGA cancer types.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Annotation scarcity limits pathology deep learning, motivating screening, generative pretraining, and transfer to segmentation.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Agent-filtered patches train a Diffusion Transformer, whose multi-level features feed a segmentation decoder.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Transferred generative features reach 55.46% mIoU on PanNuke, versus 47.19% when trained from scratch.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper concludes that generative pretraining serves both synthesis and segmentation, and lists classification and survival analysis as future work.

repos.title: Signed but Steerable: Measuring and Closing the Text-Vector Integrity Gap in Offline Retrieval-Augmented Generation
repos.paper_summary: The paper studies how far an attacker who controls the shipped vectors in a signed offline RAG knowledge pack can steer retrieval when a verifier accepts vectors within a cosine tolerance. Its margin law states that, for an optimal attacker who rotates one competing vector, the hijacked share of queries equals the fraction of angular retrieval margins below $\arccos\tau$, so exposure can be measured from honest vectors without attacking. Margins are small across SQuAD 2.0 and four BEIR corpora with two embedding models: float-noise tolerances leave up to 5.5% of queries exposed, and an INT8-calibrated threshold leaves 98–100%. On a Raspberry Pi 5 running Qwen2.5-3B, the attack lowers correct answers from 0.75 to 0.39. On a FAISS product-quantisation index of 57,638 documents, tampered vectors that pass a tolerance audit rank the attacker's document first for 25% of targets. Verifying quantisation codes with canonicalisation accepted every honest vector in the samples on three platforms. Limitations: the law covers only queries whose gold unit already ranks first, the FAISS attack is greedy and so a lower bound, guard widths are empirical, and experiments use flat indexes and synthetic update scenarios.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Signatures prove who published a knowledge pack but not that its vectors encode its text, so the paper tests that gap.

digest_headlines.heading: Background, Threat Model and Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: The threat model lets an attacker choose the vectors of review-admitted text, while verifiers recompute them or check exact codes.

digest_headlines.heading: The Margin Law
digest_headlines.headline: The margin law says an optimal attacker hijacks exactly the queries whose angular margin is below the tolerance angle, measurable without attacks.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments run on a Raspberry Pi 5, a desktop and an Apple laptop, with pinned models and a pre-registered protocol.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: At a float-noise tolerance 0–5.5% of queries stay hijackable, and at the INT8 reference threshold 98.7–100% do.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Median margins of 2.1–7.4 degrees make any tolerance's safety depend on corpus, model and storage format.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The gap can be closed by verifier-side recomputation, exact computation or code-level canonicalisation, not by tolerances.

digest_headlines.heading: Statements and Declarations
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists AI-tool use, funding, competing interests, ethics, data and code availability, and author contributions.

repos.title: LibriSpeech-Real-QA: A Benchmark for Streaming Question Answering
repos.paper_summary: LibriSpeech-Real-QA is a benchmark for event-triggered streaming speech question answering, built from LibriSpeech. Models receive audio in chunks and must respond at the moment a queried target word or semantic class (such as person names) is heard. Four tasks cover lexical and semantic detection and counting. Scoring checks both content and onset time against an acceptance window, reporting F1, recall, precision, and mean onset delay. On test-clean lexical detection, the commercial real-time APIs reach F1 of 0.78 to 0.94, but their mean onset delays are 4.84 to 5.43 s, which the authors read as responses near the end of the utterance. The authors also fine-tune Qwen2.5-Omni-7B with per-chunk SPEAK or SILENCE decisions, LoRA adapters, and negative samples. Its best lexical detection result on test-clean is F1 0.993 with a 0.661 s mean delay (400 ms chunks, +2c grace period). Its best semantic detection F1 on test-clean is 0.828. The offline baseline is not directly comparable to the streaming models. The provided text ends before the streaming results section.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing speech models respond only after a full turn, so the paper introduces LibriSpeech-Real-QA, a benchmark for event-triggered streaming interaction.

digest_headlines.heading: Benchmark Design
digest_headlines.headline: Four tasks ask models to emit target words or running counts at the moment they are heard, scored on both content and onset time.

digest_headlines.heading: Streaming Model Baseline
digest_headlines.headline: Qwen2.5-Omni-7B is finetuned to speak or stay silent at each fixed-length audio chunk, using a rebalanced loss.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: The finetuned streaming model outscores the evaluated real-time services on all four tasks, while offline inference stays stronger on counting.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Real-time services tend to respond near utterance end, while finetuning gives a causal baseline with chunk-dependent accuracy-delay trade-offs.

repos.title: A 3D foundation model unifying CT interpretation and segmentation
repos.paper_summary: HoloCT is a 3D foundation model that performs CT interpretation and voxel-level segmentation in one multimodal language model. Two parallel encoders supply whole-volume and fine-grained spatial tokens to the language model, and its segmentation tokens drive a mask decoder that returns 3D masks alongside text. It is trained on HoloDATA: 195,921 CT scans from 73 public datasets and six clinical cohorts, with 6.2 million instruction dialogues and 2.8 million CT–mask pairs. Across 346 tasks, HoloCT-8B reaches mean Dice 0.816 on 272 internal segmentation categories, versus 0.799 for 82 dataset-specific nnU-Net models. For multi-target screening, macro F1 rises from 0.368 (nnU-Net) to 0.718 internally. On CT-RATE closed-ended VQA, accuracy is 93.4% versus 84.7% for HuluMed-32B. In multicentre validation on 11,455 scans, thyroid and colon screening reaches 85.1% mean accuracy, above four radiologists in a retrospective reader study. Limitations: finding-level masks cover only chest CT; musculoskeletal bone lesions and diffuse chest findings segment less accurately; volumes are interpreted independently; and hospital validation was retrospective and within one country.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing CT models separate report text from 3D segmentation, so findings are hard to verify spatially.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: A single HoloCT model outperforms specialist and foundation models across 346 tasks, including clinical cohorts.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Mask-paired training and grounded outputs improve interpretation, but evaluation is retrospective and single-country.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: HoloCT couples dual-scale visual encoders with a multimodal language model and mask decoder, trained in three stages.

repos.title: Understanding the Out-of-Distribution Generalization of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in LLMs
repos.paper_summary: This paper analyzes chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning as compositional out-of-distribution generalization. The model sees only in-distribution single-step transitions and must solve multi-step targets whose full trajectories are never observed. A single shared step predictor is applied repeatedly. Under a clipped, bounded, Lipschitz cross-entropy loss, the target risk is at most a coefficient of order k times the sum of per-step risks, where k is the number of tokens per step and the coefficient does not depend on the number of steps T. A Rademacher-complexity bound that pools the T step datasets gives an estimation term of order sqrt(T/n), where n is the samples per step, rather than one linear in T. For autoregressive next-token prediction, the bound adds an estimation term of order k·sqrt(T/n). A parity-coupled construction shows that the sub-task empirical risk minimizer has excess risk of order sqrt(T/n) when T ≤ n. Experiments on Atom-Task and GSM8K are reported to show short-to-long and compositional generalization, and that explicit state tracking is crucial. The theory covers only supervised, explicit CoT and excludes reinforcement fine-tuning and test-time search.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Chain-of-thought generalization to unseen multi-step tasks is framed as composing reusable in-distribution step transitions.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: The setup defines a predictor applied repeatedly over a sliding window with argmax decoding and a population risk for the composite mapping.

digest_headlines.heading: Theoretical Analysis: Task Decomposition for OOD Tasks
digest_headlines.headline: Composite CoT risk is bounded by a depth-independent multiple of summed step risks, plus an estimation term growing as root T over n.

digest_headlines.heading: Specific Analysis: Results in the Next-Token Prediction Setting
digest_headlines.headline: Next-token prediction training inherits the bound, with an excess term of order k times the square root of T over n.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On Atom-Task, CoT-trained models generalize from short training chains to longer unseen compositions, unlike models trained without intermediate steps.

digest_headlines.heading: Further Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work spans CoT prompting and training, while prior CoT theory is qualitative or limited to narrow or two-step settings.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Reusing one transition model explains CoT's out-of-distribution gain, though the theory excludes reinforcement fine-tuning and test-time search.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding
digest_headlines.headline: Funding came from Jiangsu programs, Chinese ministry plans and Singapore Management University, and the conference reviewers are thanked.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives the decoder architecture and derives the covering-number bound behind the Rademacher complexity term.

repos.title: DreamRealm: Exploring and Materializing Hallucination Worlds for Trustworthy Vision-Language Models
repos.paper_summary:
DreamRealm is a post-training framework that teaches a multimodal model to match its own hallucinated answers to the edited images that make them correct. Its pipeline, RealmForgePipe, mines wrong answers from the target model through high-temperature sampling and likelihood ranking, then uses a verifier and an image-editing model to make minimal edits that validate each answer. The resulting RealmSet has 28,960 human-approved edited examples across 22 categories, built from Qwen3.5-9B. The objective, RealmMatch, adds supervised learning on matched pairs to bidirectional contrastive losses over an image–response likelihood matrix.

On six perception and hallucination benchmarks, DreamRealm improves Qwen3.5-9B on all seven reported metrics, with gains of 7.26 percentage points on HallusionBench accuracy and 11.34 percentage points on MMVP pair accuracy. Ablations indicate that observed and latent hallucinations supply complementary data, and that RealmMatch outperforms SFT, DPO, and GRPO on most metrics. Models trained on the Qwen-mined data (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Gemma-4-E4B-it, InternVL3.5-8B) improve less, so their hallucination spaces are not fully interchangeable.

Limitations: data construction requires GPT-Image generation and human review, and some scenes remain hard to edit successfully.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Visual hallucinations persist, and existing post-training rarely builds supervision around the model's own perceptual confusions.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work corrects responses under fixed images or builds visual contrasts from retrieved or generated images, not from the target model's hallucinations.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 Method
digest_headlines.headline: RealmForgePipe mines and edits hallucinations, and RealmMatch trains a likelihood matrix with bidirectional contrastive losses to assign responses to images.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: DreamRealm improves all seven Qwen3.5-9B metrics, and ablations show latent hallucinations add gains beyond observed errors.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Data construction is costly, and the image-editing model's limits leave some scenes hard to edit.

digest_headlines.heading: 6 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Authors conclude that hallucination assignment shows potential to improve visual perception and mitigate hallucinations across benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists the editing algorithm, mining and editing examples, category statistics, annotation protocol, a worked example, training settings, and qualitative comparisons.
